files.text:
On a cold window

The Weather on the Glass

Condensation, rain, and the street beyond going soft.

Glass in winter is the coldest thing in a warm room. The air that touches it is chilled below its dew point and has to let go of some of the water it was carrying, and the water comes out on the pane as droplets, hundreds of thousands to the square centimetre, each far too small to see. Every one of them is a little lens. Light passing through is bent off at a slant, and with so many lenses bending it every way at once the street outside turns into a soft, bright weather of its own: still lit, no longer drawn.

The mist is never even. It lies thickest along the bottom of the pane and into the corners, where the frame holds the cold, and thins toward the top, where the warm air of the room rises past it. Low down the droplets grow until they touch and run together, and now and then one becomes heavy enough to slide, cutting a clean channel down to the sill.

Outside it is raining, and the rain sits on the glass in separate drops, big enough to see and smooth enough to be lenses in earnest. Each holds the whole street in miniature and upside down, the pale sky pooled in its lower half and the roofs hanging from the top. A drop clings until it is heavy enough, then lets go all at once, stops, slips again, and gathers up every smaller drop in its way, leaving a clean track behind it that the drizzle slowly fills.

Gustave Caillebotte painted this crossing in 1877, when it was barely ten years old. The quarter behind the Gare Saint-Lazare had gone up in a hurry, its streets laid out like the spokes of a wheel and named after the capitals of Europe: here the rue de Turin and the rue de Saint-Pétersbourg meet, and the corner building stands at the point between them like the prow of a ship. Everything is new and grey and wet. The paving stones shine. A man in a top hat and a woman with a pearl at her ear come toward us under one umbrella, so close and so large on a canvas more than two and a half metres wide that they seem about to walk out of it.

Caillebotte lived not far away, and few painters looked at Paris through glass as often as he did: his brother standing at the window of the family flat, a man on a balcony over the boulevard, the street seen straight down from above with its trees and its benches. Here he is down in the rain with everyone else, but the picture keeps the cool, even light of a window on a wet day, and the far end of the street goes into the same pale grey as the sky.

Write on a pane with a finger and the words stay longer than you would think. The fingertip leaves a film of oil behind it, too thin to see, and the next time the window fogs the water gathers differently on that film, in fewer and larger drops, so the letters come back as a ghost in the mist, weeks later, for someone else to find. Wipe a clear patch and the cold starts at once to take it back, from the edges inward.

draw on the glass

# window-pane A painting seen through a cold window on a wet day. The inside of the glass is misted with condensation, a luminous grey that turns the street into soft shapes of light; rain sits on the outside in drops, each a little lens holding the street upside down, and now and then a heavy one lets go, stops, slips again and runs down, gathering the small ones. Press and drag (or, on a phone, stroke sideways, or hold still a moment and then draw) and your finger wipes a clear streak with a ragged edge and a line of pushed-up droplets; the street is sharp behind it, still behind the rain. Over twenty seconds or so the cold takes it back, from the edges in, and leaves a ghost of what you wrote. The glass has been used before: a broad diagonal sweep someone made to look out, a finger dragged off its edge, drips run down from it, half fogged back. ```html ``` The `` sizes the pane. Leave it at its natural ratio, or give the figure a height and the img `object-fit: cover` (and any `object-position`); the glass takes exactly the same crop. `class="wp-bleed"` makes a full-bleed band (`92svh`, or `72svh` on a portrait screen, so a landscape picture keeps about half its width in view). Or call `windowPane(figure, options)` yourself; it returns `destroy()`. The module also exports `cursive(word, x, y, xHeight, perPoint)`, joined handwriting (letters h, e, l, o) as an array of points: handy for tests, and for `data-writing`. ## Options | attribute | option | default | | |---|---|---|---| | `data-mist` | `mist` | `0.85` | 0-1, how thick the condensation is | | `data-rain` | `rain` | `0.5` | 0-1, how hard it is raining: new drops and drizzle | | `data-refog` | `refog` | `22` | seconds for a wipe to fog over again; `0` = never | | `data-wiped` | `wiped` | `1` | a broad wipe made earlier, half fogged back, with drips; `0` for clean mist | | `data-writing` | `writing` | `""` | a word already written there too, half fogged over (h e l o only) | | `data-seed` | `seed` | `3` | the rain and the grain of the mist | The options object wins over the attributes. ## Theming | variable | default | | |---|---|---| | `--wp-floor` | `#b9b6b0` | behind the image while it loads | | `--wp-cursor` | `default` | the cursor over the glass | There is no colour to set: the mist is made from the painting's own light, greyed, so it suits whatever is behind it. Pick a smooth, finished picture (a townscape, a harbour, a street): behind a wipe it is seen nearly 1:1, where heavy impasto reads as paint, not as a view. Strong darks and a pale sky show the drops best. ## How it works One WebGL2 context, three kinds of water. - **The street.** The painting is cropped to the canvas (object-fit honoured) at one texel per device pixel, with mipmaps, and read through a wipe with half a level of mip bias at DPR 2 (the street through glass, not the weave of the canvas). Three blurred copies are made once, on the GPU, with a separable 25-tap Gaussian: sigma 0.15% and 0.46% of the pane's width (at least 1.5 and 4 px), so the street keeps its big shapes through the mist, and 80 px for the colour of the veil. - **Mist** is a density map on the CPU, about one cell per 3 css px, four channels uploaded as one RGBA texture: mist, the rim of droplets pushed up by a finger, the wet film it leaves (dries in ~5 s), and the oily trace it leaves for good. The density seen is the map times a base that is thicker at the bottom and sides and drifts slowly (two noise layers moving with time). Light through it is the physics of a scattering layer: a fraction `exp(-6.5 · density)` comes through unscattered and sharp, the rest is the blur; then a veil (the 80 px blur, greyed and lifted) for light scattered back toward the eye. Up close it is droplets: a 512² wrapping tile of a few thousand non-overlapping circles (a breath figure), each a tiny normal-mapped lens that catches light above it and darkens at its edge, with larger beads low on the pane, on oily traces and along a wipe's rim. The tile's gaps let a little more of the sharp street through, which is the grain you see. - **Wiping** stamps a capsule along the pointer path (coalesced events, a stamp per 0.8 cells) with a fingertip radius that wanders a little along the stroke. Mist inside goes, a thin ring outside takes what was pushed (in proportion to how foggy it was there), and the shader roughens the border at the droplets' own scale. Refog is two terms: haze nucleating everywhere at a mottled rate (slow at first, then thickening), and fog creeping in from the edges (it grows only toward its neighbours' level). Only the changing region is updated. - **Ghosts.** The oily trace makes later fog thinner and coarser, so writing comes back as a ghost after it refogs, as it does on a real window. - **Rain** follows Lucas Bebber's *Rain & Water Effect* (Codrops, 2015), rewritten in css px: drops land with a size distribution skewed small; heavy ones get random kicks of momentum (stick, slip) and wander as they run (a random walk plus a pull toward the biggest droplet just below, which they swallow), leave beads of uneven size at uneven intervals (exponential spacing, a third skipped) that slowly dry away so old trails break into gaps, merge with what they touch (area conserved, bigger one moves toward the smaller) and get a kick from it, and clear the fine drizzle in a track that the drizzle refills. Drops and drizzle (a few thousand) are drawn each frame as instanced quads into a mipmapped texture: normal, height, cover. Running drops stretch and their trailing top narrows; still ones have slightly irregular outlines. - **A drop** samples the sharp painting at `uv - normal · reach` (reach is a fifth of the short side), so it shows the street inverted and minified, and the mip level the GPU picks from that steep gradient keeps tiny drops from sparkling. Then a dark rim, light gathered into its lower inner edge, a highlight, and a soft shadow under it from a blurred mip of the cover. Through the mist, a drop 4 mm behind it is softened only a little (its own mip level 1-3), unlike the street 40 m behind it. - **Drips.** A fresh wipe longer than ~60 px sends one or two drips down from its lowest edge after a moment: a bead that runs in stops and starts for 20-110 px, carving a narrow channel through the fog, and slowly shrinks. A few old runs are already on the glass at the bottom of the pane. ## Tuning Mist look: `base`, the transmission `exp(-6.5 · densL)` and the veil mix in the `COMP` shader. Rain: `minR`/`maxR` (3 and 15 css px, scaled by pane size) in `layout()`, spawn rates and the slip threshold (`maxR · 0.45`) in `stepRain()`. Refog: `U` (nucleation) and `Gr` (edge creep) in `refog()`. Fingertip: `finger` in `layout()` (9-15 px for a mouse) and `tip` in `strokeStart()` (12-16 px for a finger). The earlier wipe (its sweep, the two finger streaks and the drips) and how far it has fogged back are in `prepare()`; it refogs at 7% of the normal rate until someone wipes over it. ## Behaviour and cost - A loop draws about 30 frames a second while the pane is on screen (the rain is always moving). Off screen or in a hidden tab, nothing runs. - Startup is one long task of about 0.3 s on a laptop (blurs, droplet tile, and 20 s of rain simulated unseen so the glass is already wet). A frame costs one instanced draw of a few thousand quads, a mipmap of it, and one full-screen pass of about fifteen texture reads; CPU work is under 2 ms. - Canvas DPR is capped at 2. The image should be at least twice the pane's css width (the demo's is 2968 px). - Without WebGL2, or if the image is cross-origin (WebGL refuses it), the `` simply stays. If the GPU drops the context the img shows until it comes back. A resize rebuilds the glass (a phone toolbar sliding away does not). ## Accessibility, touch and reduced motion - The image is decorative (`alt=""`), the canvas `aria-hidden`; nothing is focusable, so keyboard users simply move past it. - Touch never traps the page: the figure is `touch-action: pan-y`. A vertical swipe scrolls. A sideways stroke wipes at once. A press held still for 250 ms enters free drawing in any direction for that touch only, and only then are its moves kept from scrolling. Long-press callouts are off. - `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: a still frame of misted glass with drops and the half-fogged earlier wipe. Wiping still works (it is direct manipulation) and stays; nothing refogs, drips or rains. - Print shows the plain image. ## Credits - Gustave Caillebotte, *Paris Street; Rainy Day*, 1877. The Art Institute of Chicago, public domain (CC0 image), via its IIIF server.
